title: I'm developing a 2D isometric historical city builder using Codex
author: Odd_Revolution7522
selftext:
This idea has been on my mind for years.

I’ve always been slightly frustrated that most city builders are essentially “Brasília Simulator: The Game”: you begin in a specific era, on an empty map, and build a city from scratch.

I wanted to try something different: developing the same settlement across seven ages, from the Paleolithic to the Modern Age, on a single persistent map. Buildings, resources, technologies, and the needs of your population evolve, but the history and layout of the city remain visible throughout the game.

I’ve been working on it for about a month, and the first three ages are now ready to test, its based on Paris :

[https://pixel-metropolis.com/](https://pixel-metropolis.com/)

Almost everything has been generated with Codex and GPT-5.6 Sol, including the code, visual assets, and music, with a few CC0 sprites and sound effects mixed in.

The process has gone surprisingly smoothly so far. The most persistent challenge has been getting image generation to respect a consistent 2:1 isometric perspective. Small deviations quickly become obvious once assets are placed next to one another. I eventually created a custom generation and validation workflow for this, which has helped tremendously.

There are still rough edges, but the core progression is playable. I’d be very interested in feedback, especially on the first-time experience, the transition between ages, and whether the central idea feels compelling after playing for a while.

I've been dabbling in gamedev on Android then in Unity for 10 years and I've always got discouraged after the prototype phase, I'm so happy that with AI we can now concentrate on game design instead of losing weeks designing menus !

comments.author: OkRepresentative7420
comments.body: Great work. Do you mind sharing how you approached the asset generation pipeline? Im building an isometric RTS game and any help would be greatly appreciated.

replies.author: Odd_Revolution7522
replies.body:
No problem, so here is how I approach it typically when adding a new asset : 

1. Define the art direction of the era. For the Metal Age for example, I wanted a gaulish/celtic mix of architecture and historical references. The output is a brief + color palette for all buildings.

2. This is the most important step to ensure asset consistency : give the AI a screen capture of the game with existing buildings and the isometric grid on, then ask it to put the new concept building in the screen capture. This ensures consistency with other assets and angle coherence, since the model will generate the new model along the grid. (attached an example of when I asked it to create a stone mason building).

3. Then ask the model to take this image as reference and generate the SW orientation (in HD). Validate or rework, then ask to generate the rear view and validate or iterate as well. This is the step where geometry and relative scale can go wonky, be ruthless here and don't hesitate to restart from the SW orientation if the result isn't good. Color palette and lighting drift can be fixed later.

4. Once both front and rear views are validated, mirror them to generate the full 4 orientations atlas. It's important here to have a defined contract of atlas size vs building ingame footprint to avoid scale and detail-per-pixel discrepancies between assets. Just ask the model to generate a global contract, it should handle it fine.

5. Post production : many times the model confuses directions, I just use Piskel to swap orientations and have them be consistent (my atlases are all SW/SE/NW/NE). Once the asset is ingame, I rework chroma/saturation/luminosity etc for consistency, or just ask the model to handle it deterministically sometimes.

  
Let me know if it helps !

https://preview.redd.it/5yy25r71pgnh1.png?width=2516&format=png&auto=webp&s=f4e4e5e263f1e77630ac5fb32d153c2fa3e0357d

replies.author: RustOceanX
replies.body:
Perhaps the following workflow would also be interesting: Have the AI in Blender create the object using simple basic shapes. Then have the AI render the object in Blender from any direction using an isometric camera perspective. Feed the rendered image from Blender to the AI and have it generate a detailed 2D render from it. The developers at Factorio do this as well, but without AI and using detailed 3D models. They then animate and render it in Blender to create the 2D sprites.

The advantage of using 3D models in Blender is that the perspective and view are very easy to control, and you can supplement the 3D models yourself with simple 3D shapes and tell the AI, for example, “Turn the green box on the building into a cannon.”

replies.author: Odd_Revolution7522
replies.body:
I think its important to be a bit knowledgeable about gamedev beforehand.

It teaches you to decompose problems and orient the model to the correct solution space.

For instance there is a huge difference between telling a model : 

"Make the villagers stop walking over buildings and rivers" and "Implement async A\* for villagers pathfinding with cached and reused paths".

Knowledge about systems and architecture is also very important, otherwise you end up with three different implementations for what is essentially the same problem.

I think my top 3 requests are : "reuse and extend X system" and "make it modular and agnostic".

I also regularly ask the model to reaudit the code to spot god classes, bad performance and code that isn't properly decoupled.

For the web browser part, its very easy, chatgpt released "Sites", which is a free hosting solution for your Codex projects, you can query "@Sites" within Codex.
